notes: RBox revision of the topic's functional relation (RBOX_PER_TOPIC: functional). Functionality of in_genus holds without exception: under the zoological and botanical codes a species name is a binomen, one genus name plus one epithet, so a species is placed in exactly one genus at a time (taxonomists may disagree about which genus, but no classification puts a species in two). The edit is stated in plain words ('can belong to more than one genus at the same time') rather than as "'Belongs to the genus' is not functional": with that wording 3 of 4 models missed the negation ('Is it false that ... is not functional?'), and the plain one has no double negative. The direct question was 'Does each species belong to at most one genus?'; it now asks the edited possibility directly. Instances moved from the lion and the gray wolf, whose genera (and non-genera) are famous enough to decide the answer on their own (reviewer flags), to two little-known carnivorans: the fossa of Madagascar (genus Cryptoprocta; Eupleres is another Malagasy carnivoran genus) and the olinguito (genus Bassaricyon, described in 2013; Nasua is the coati genus in the same family). Both are asked as 'Is it consistent with this fact that ...?', no then yes, the wording of geography-replace-0018. The cross-lingual queries ask the first instance and keep the genus names in Latin, as taxonomy does in every language. Near unrelated asks the same property (functionality) of a biology relation the genus rank cannot reach, the biological mother of an animal (a leak turns no to yes); it replaced 'Can one species belong to two different families?', which sits downstream of the edit (genus membership chains into family, so two genera could properly give two families). Far asks a different property of an unrelated relation.

The fossa belongs to the genus Cryptopro.why: True: the fossa, Cryptoprocta ferox, is the only living species of its genus. The sentence form is rare; the binomial is the usual way the fact is written.
